bibliography.abstract: Abstract In the early 2000s, various jurisdictions across the United States initiated Safe Routes to School (SRTS) programs to improve students’ safety when walking or biking to school. For many areas, SRTS programs involve identifying safety risk issues such as missing sidewalks, unconnected trails, high crossing speeds, or faded crosswalks and implementing corresponding measures. Such SRTS programs prioritize projects using overall benefit and cost–benefit criteria; however, limited empirical evidence explains which types of safety recommendations are most likely to rank highly under each criterion and how these rankings influence review and implementation decisions of such projects. This study addresses this gap by evaluating 4,654 SRTS recommendations from 137 schools in Austin, TX (2016–2023) to examine the relationship between project type, benefit ranking, cost–benefit evaluation, and implementation outcomes. Text network analysis identified nine major project categories. Mixed-effects ordered logit models show substantial variation in benefit rankings across project types. Bike facilities exhibit the strongest association with high overall benefit (OR = 13.6), followed by trail connections (OR = 6.57) and speed-related measures (OR = 6.33). Difficult crossings (OR = 4.52) and faded crosswalk markings (OR = 4.15) also demonstrate elevated benefit likelihoods. In contrast, cost–benefit rankings differ markedly: faded crosswalk improvements and difficult crossing treatments show the highest cost–benefit associations, while speed-related measures remain favorable (OR = 2.10). Bike facilities and trail connections display negative cost–benefit coefficients, reflecting lower economic efficiency despite high perceived benefits. Mixed-effects binary logit models indicate that implementation aligns more closely with cost–benefit than overall benefit rankings. Speed-related projects are 2.21 times more likely to be implemented, whereas bike facilities and trail connections are 53% and 65% less likely to be implemented, respectively. Overall, high cost–benefit recommendations consistently demonstrate higher probabilities of review and implementation. Theoretically, this study clarifies the divergence between safety benefit and economic efficiency in SRTS prioritization. Practically, it provides a data-driven framework to support transparent and balanced decision-making in school-route safety planning.

en.caveats: The findings are based on a single city's SRTS program and administrative decisions, which may reflect local funding structures and political priorities unique to Austin, Texas.
en.what: This study analyzed 4,654 Safe Routes to School (SRTS) recommendations across 137 schools in Austin, Texas, spanning 2016 to 2023, to understand how project types influence prioritization and actual implementation. Using text network analysis and mixed-effects logit models, the researchers found that while bike facilities and trail connections have the highest perceived safety benefits (odds ratios of 13.6 and 6.57), they have low cost-benefit rankings and are 53% and 65% less likely to be implemented. Conversely, speed-related measures and crosswalk improvements are highly favored for implementation due to superior cost-benefit scores, with speed-related projects being 2.21 times more likely to be built.
en.why: It reveals a systematic disconnect in municipal planning where infrastructure projects with the highest safety benefits are routinely passed over for implementation in favor of cheaper, more economically efficient alternatives.
